problem: 'Later that morning' contradicts 3.19, which has Jane up and dressed 'by noon' earlier the same day; the doctor's visit then reads as happening before the scene just described.
new_text: "Come now, Miss Jane, don't cry," said Bessie when she finished. She might as well have told the fire not to burn. But how could she have known the depth of suffering I was enduring? Later that day, Mr. Lloyd came again.

problem: 'Guy Fawkes' will not be known to many modern (especially non-British) readers; the joke depends on knowing he was a conspirator. A brief in-line gloss keeps the joke.
new_text: Bessie invited him into the breakfast room and led the way out. In the conversation that followed between him and Mrs. Reed, I gathered from what happened afterward that the apothecary suggested I be sent to school. The suggestion was no doubt eagerly accepted, because as Abbot said when discussing it with Bessie one night while they sewed in the nursery—after I was in bed and, they assumed, asleep—"The Missus was, I dare say, glad enough to get rid of such a tiresome, ill-natured child, who always looked as if she were watching everybody and scheming behind their backs." Abbot, I think, gave me credit for being a sort of infant Guy Fawkes—a little plotter in the household.

problem: 'a small closet to sleep in' reads today as a cupboard/wardrobe; the period sense is a small room.
new_text: From my conversation with Mr. Lloyd and from the discussion between Bessie and Abbot that I overheard, I gathered enough hope to make me want to get well. A change seemed near, and I longed for it in silence. But it was slow in coming. Days and weeks passed. I regained my normal health, but no one mentioned the subject I was constantly thinking about. Mrs. Reed watched me sometimes with a stern eye but rarely spoke to me. Since my illness, she had drawn an even sharper line between me and her own children, giving me a small closet of a room to sleep in alone, making me eat my meals by myself and spend all my time in the nursery while my cousins stayed in the drawing room. She dropped no hint about sending me to school, yet I felt instinctively certain she wouldn't keep me under her roof much longer. Her glance, more than ever, expressed a deep and fixed aversion when it fell on me.

problem: 'abandoned' in its period sense (depraved) will be heard as 'deserted', which is confusing for an orphan narrator.
new_text: Mrs. Reed quickly recovered herself. She shook me hard, boxed both my ears, and left without a word. Bessie filled the gap with an hour-long lecture, proving beyond doubt that I was the most wicked and depraved child ever raised under a roof. I half believed her, because all I could feel were dark emotions surging inside me.

problem: Jane is standing outside the breakfast room, but the text says she is afraid to go forward 'to the parlor', which sounds like a different room.
new_text: I now stood in the empty hall. Before me was the breakfast room door, and I stopped, intimidated and trembling. What a miserable little coward fear and unjust punishment had made of me in those days! I was afraid to go back to the nursery and afraid to go forward into the breakfast room. For ten minutes I stood in anxious indecision. The fierce ringing of the breakfast room bell decided it—I had to go in.

problem: 'set on the shaft as its capital' — the architectural term 'capital' will be heard by listeners as 'capital city'. Plainer wording keeps the image.
new_text: "Who could want me?" I asked myself, as I turned the stiff door handle with both hands. It resisted for a second or two. "What will I see besides Aunt Reed in there? A man or a woman?" The handle turned, the door opened, and passing through with a low curtsy, I looked up at—a black pillar! That, at least, was what it looked like at first glance: a straight, narrow, black-clad shape standing stiffly on the rug. The grim face at the top was like a carved mask set on top of the pillar.

problem: 'I will remember how you shoved me back ... and locked me in there, until my dying day' — the time phrase at the end attaches to 'locked me in', so it can sound as if she was locked in until her dying day. Move it next to 'remember'.
new_text: "How dare I, Mrs. Reed? How dare I? Because it is the truth. You think I have no feelings and that I can survive without a single bit of love or kindness. But I cannot live like that, and you have no pity. I will remember until my dying day how you shoved me back—roughly and violently shoved me back—into the red room and locked me in there. Even though I was in agony. Even though I cried out, while choking with distress, 'Have mercy! Have mercy, Aunt Reed!' And that punishment you gave me because your wicked boy hit me—knocked me down for nothing. I will tell anyone who asks the exact truth. People think you're a good woman, but you are bad and hard-hearted. You are the deceitful one!"
